newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Europe-Asia business summit to open amid successes.
newsitem.headline: Europe-Asia business summit to open amid successes.

text.p: The World Economic Forum (WEF) will open its Europe/East Asia conference next week happy in the knowledge that the meeting in its present form may be outgrowing its usefulness.

This year's three-day conference includes sessions on the state of the world economy, financial flows and stock markets in Asia and expectations heading into the World Trade Organisation meeting in Singapore in December.

But the growing dialogue between European and Asian leaders means the need for a business forum that concentrates primarily on the relationship between the two regions has diminished, said Claude Smadja, managing director for the WEF.
"Now that this process has been launched, we are less concerned about the Europe-Asia link," Smadja told Reuters in an interview.
The WEF, which comprises 1,100 member companies, will hold its fifth annual conference to bring together Europe and Asian political and business leaders on November 18-20 in Hong Kong.

The Geneva-based forum, also known the Davos forum for the annual meeting it organises at the Swiss ski resort, groups political and business leaders for discussions on selected economic and political themes.

The Europe/East Asia conferences originally were designed to help redress imbalances in a triangular relationship in which the United States had strong ties with both Europe and Asia but the Europe-Asia link was weak.
Smadja noted that the conference already welcomes participants from the United States as well as other countries outside Asia and Europe and "that trend seems to be developing."

Smadja said the WEF can claim a large share of the credit for the inaugural Asia-Europe Meeting (ASEM) of top officals held last March in Bangkok. He said the group strongly recommended such a meeting in 1994.
At the close of ASEM, delegates said the conference went a long way toward bridging gaps between the two regions.
Still, thorny issues relating to human rights and cultural values continue to irritate leaders in both Asia and Europe.
Smadja said he does not expect politics to mar next week's WEF meeting. Tension and outright clashes were not unusual five years ago, but disagreements are more low key now, he said.

"Some Westerners had a way of being patronising, but they realised that being patronising is not useful. At the same time, the spectacular growth in Asia had created a sort of arrogance among Asians, with many saying that Europeans are too soft, too lazy. And that was not very helpful," said Smadja.
"Now there is a much more mature relationship and we have seen that evolve over the last five years," he said.

The fact that heads of state and other top brass will be in Manila for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting and not in Hong Kong means that political talk at the WEF summit will be minimised, Smadja acknowledged.
But he stressed that real dialogue between Europe and Asia can't happen unless business takes a higher profile.
"Governments have to create the environment but they can't do the job without the business people," he said.
This year's meeting will take a look at the economic outlook for Asia, Europe and the rest of the world, but many of the sessions are dedicated to business opportunities and strategies.
For example, officials from China's provinces will reveal "what makes or breaks a deal or a joint venture", said Smadja.
